title: Wi-Fi Basics: Bands, Channels, Signal and Security
oneLiner: Why Wi-Fi slows down when it's busy, why channels 1, 6 and 11, what -67 dBm means, and which security mode a company network should use.
keyTakeaway: Wi-Fi is a shared radio channel: only one device on a channel transmits at a time, and overlapping channels turn into noise. Plan non-overlapping channels, use 5 or 6 GHz for capacity, design for a signal of about -67 dBm or better, and use WPA2 or WPA3 Enterprise so every user has their own credentials.
explanation:
Wi-Fi (the IEEE 802.11 standards) carries Ethernet frames over radio. An access point (AP) is the base station devices connect to, and the SSID is the network name it advertises. Unlike a switch port, the air is shared: on any one channel only one device can transmit at a time, and everyone else waits. More devices or more access points on the same channel means less airtime for each.

Frequencies come in bands. 2.4 GHz travels furthest and through walls best, but only has room for three channels that don't overlap (1, 6 and 11), and it's shared with Bluetooth, microwave ovens and every neighbour. 5 GHz has around two dozen channels and much more capacity at shorter range, and 6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7) adds a clean, wide band for newer devices. Two access points within earshot on overlapping channels interfere: each hears the other's transmissions as noise it can't decode. On the same channel they at least take turns.

Signal strength is measured in dBm, decibels relative to one milliwatt. The numbers are negative and logarithmic: -50 is strong, -67 is the usual target for reliable voice and video, below -80 is barely usable, and every 10 dB is a factor of 10 in power. Walls, metal racking, machinery and people absorb signal, so industrial sites need a site survey rather than a guess.

For security, WEP is broken and must never be used. WPA2-Personal and WPA3-Personal use one shared passphrase (WPA3's SAE handshake resists offline guessing). Company networks should use Enterprise mode, 802.1X, where each user or device authenticates individually against a RADIUS server, so someone who leaves can be cut off without changing everyone's password. Plan three access points below, then see what a signal level means.
